title: Though the fig tree (Habakkuk 3:17–19)
hook: no fruit, no flock, and yet I will rejoice

segments.voice: Yesterday, little Bethlehem, the hillside village Micah pointed to. Your line: the least of the towns.

A prophet's usual job is to speak to the people for God. Habakkuk talks back to God. His book opens with a complaint, in the King James Bible: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" Violence everywhere, the law ignored, the wicked winning. God's answer makes it worse: the Babylonians are coming, a fierce army that will sweep through like the desert wind. So Habakkuk climbs a watchtower, in his words, to wait and see what God will say. Three short chapters later, he comes down singing.

The song ends with Habakkuk imagining the worst. In the King James: "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls." Count it. Figs, grapes, olives, grain, sheep, cattle. For a farming people, that's everything: the pantry, the bank account, the retirement plan. Then one small word: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation." Yet. Habakkuk doesn't say things will turn out fine, or that the fig tree will bloom after all. He says: even if it doesn't. His joy is anchored somewhere the harvest can't reach. Then the last picture: "he will make my feet like hinds' feet." A hind is a female deer, and in those hills deer pick their way up steep, rocky slopes without falling. The ground doesn't get easier. The feet get surer. The book ends with a note for the choir leader about stringed instruments: this cry of faith from the edge of disaster was meant to be sung together. Some Christians turn to these verses in hard seasons, and some read Habakkuk as a pattern for honest prayer: complain first, wait on the watchtower, then sing. The yet doesn't cancel the complaint. It comes after it.
screen: `NOT IF IT BLOOMS. EVEN IF IT DOESN'T.`
`FEET LIKE A DEER'S ON THE ROCKS.`
then, large: `YET I WILL REJOICE IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: If today is hard, let it be hard, and name what's not blooming, money, health, a relationship, plans that fell apart, plainly, the way Habakkuk listed his empty fields. Then look for one thing that's still good, a person who loves you, light through a window, a song you know by heart, and rest your attention there. If you pray, say Habakkuk's yet in your own heart; if not, let that one good thing be enough for now.
Hinds' feet. What Habakkuk says God gives him for climbing steep, rocky ground: not an easier path, but surer footing.
Your line: yet I will rejoice. The ground stays steep; the feet get surer. That's day four hundred ninety-one.

screen: `DAY 491 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HE WILL SING OVER YOU.`

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Habakkuk 3:17–18 in times of loss, and its words have been set in hymns and songs; Habakkuk 2:4, on the just living by faith, is quoted in Romans, Galatians and Hebrews.

fork.setup: you're a farmer. the figs didn't blossom, the olives failed, the sheep are gone. what does Habakkuk do?
options: name it all, and rejoice anyway.
fork.reveal: he lists every loss honestly, and then says "yet I will rejoice in the LORD." the yet comes after the complaint, not instead of it.

original.note: Hebrew: but I, yet I. the first word of Habakkuk 3:18, the turn of the whole song.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful verse about staying positive.
what it means: a prophet names total loss honestly, every crop and every flock, and still chooses joy in God.
what a scholar hears: the book moves from complaint to watchtower to song, and ends with a note for the choir leader, so it was meant for worship.

chat.says: Does Habakkuk promise that the hard times will turn out fine if you trust God?
options: No. He says even if the fig tree doesn't bloom, yet I will rejoice.
Yes. He says the fig tree will bloom again before the army arrives.
No. He says to stop complaining and pretend that everything is fine.
chat.meaning: Habakkuk lists every failed harvest, then says yet I will rejoice. His joy is anchored where the harvest can't reach.

Habakkuk.meaning: a prophet who talks back to God, then sings

hind.meaning: a female deer, sure-footed on steep, rocky slopes

notes: Habakkuk 2:4 is quoted in Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11 and Hebrews 10:38 ('three times'). Confirm.
'Fields shall yield no meat': 'meat' means food/grain in the KJV; rendered as grain in the count. Confirm.
Habakkuk 3:19's closing note 'To the chief singer on my stringed instruments' paraphrased as a note for the choir leader.
Original: וַאֲנִי opens 3:18 in the Masoretic text. Confirm pointing.
'Leaned on these verses for centuries, in famines, prisons and hospital rooms' is general and unsourced; soften if needed.
